concept_name: Bond Polarity and Dipole Moment — Shape Determines Molecular Polarity
section: Class 11 Chemistry Ch.4 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', §4.4 — Polarity of Bonds and Dipole Moment
source_book: NCERT Chemistry Class 11, Ch.4 'Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure', §4.4 — chapter-index scope reference only; teaching, sequence, examples and phrasing authored from first principles. NCERT Exemplar consulted for misconception beliefs only (bond-polarity-implies-molecular-polarity, lone-pair-adds-not-opposes); no problem text, figure or prose imported. Desk 1, concept 1 of 2 in the Phase-0 bonding wave — the first bond_polarity_dipole_moment build on the bonding_scene scenario (field_3d, scenario capabilities E1 + E2 + E1c).

real_world_anchor.primary: A microwave oven's field flips direction billions of times a second. Water molecules are tiny dipoles — a delta-minus oxygen end and delta-plus hydrogen ends — so each flip turns them, and that turning is heat. That is why water-rich food gets hot in a microwave while a dry ceramic plate stays cool: dielectric heating only works on a molecule that has a dipole in the first place, and that dipole exists only because water is bent, not because its bonds happen to be polar.
real_world_anchor.secondary: Oil and water do not mix. Polar molecules attract each other more strongly than they attract nonpolar molecules, so the two liquids stay separate instead of blending — the same dipole that makes water heat in a microwave is why it separates from oil.

delta_chi.name: electronegativity difference between the two bonded atoms

bond_moment_intrinsic.name: intrinsic (per-bond) dipole moment, table-ratified against CRC gas-phase data and a four-vector solve for nitrogen

lone_pair_moment_N.name: nitrogen lone-pair dipole moment (the sole central atom with an explicit, non-zero lone-pair term)

mu.name: molecular dipole moment (the resultant)
mu.derived: vector sum of every bond dipole plus (nitrogen only) the lone-pair dipole

bond_angle.name: the bonded angle at the central atom

ligand.name: the halogen swapped into the H-X slot

spin.name: rotation about the vertical axis, teacher-driven when live

formulas.delta_chi: |chi_A - chi_B|  (reference only -- bonding_scene computes this natively, not via PM_interpolate)
formulas.bond_dipole_vector: bond_moment_intrinsic * unit_vector(central -> ligand)  (sign convention: positive = central atom is delta+)
formulas.molecular_dipole: mu = |sum_i(bond_dipole_vector_i) + lone_pair_moment_N * unit_vector(central -> lone_pair)|  (the lone-pair term is 0 for every central atom except nitrogen)

constraints: mu is the VECTOR sum of every bond dipole plus any explicit lone-pair dipole, never their arithmetic (scalar) sum
every bond arrow is drawn delta-plus to delta-minus; the convention is asserted once (STATE_2 narration) and holds unchanged in every later state
a molecule with n identical bonds in a fully symmetric point-group arrangement (linear AB2, tetrahedral AB4) has mu = 0 regardless of individual bond polarity
the higher-delta-chi bond in any displayed pair carries the longer arrow (STATE_2's core rule); STATE_7's four-vector ratification exists specifically to keep this true for nitrogen
changing or removing exactly one bond's contribution (STATE_6's Cl -> H swap) changes the resultant by exactly that one bond's vector delta -- the other bonds' vectors are untouched
no chemical reaction, state symbol, oxidation number, or mole-scale factor appears anywhere in this concept

ratified reference values (engine BS_BOND_MOMENT_D / BS_LONE_PAIR_D, bond_polarity_dipole_moment R1/R2/R3): HCl delta_chi=0.96; HF mu=1.83 D delta_chi=1.78; HCl mu=1.11 D delta_chi=0.96; HBr mu=0.83 D delta_chi=0.76; HI mu=0.45 D delta_chi=0.46; CO2 mu=0.00 D; H2O mu=1.85 D at bond angle 104.5 deg; CCl4 mu=0.00 D; CHCl3 mu=1.04 D (ratified per-molecule override, Cl bond moment 0.74 D on both CCl4 and CHCl3); NH3 mu=1.47 D delta_chi=0.84 (lone pair adds to the bond resultant); NF3 mu=0.23 D delta_chi=0.94 (lone pair opposes the bond resultant)

concept_tier_note: Tier: one star, not diamond. STATE_5 (CCl4, four bond dipoles summing to exactly zero in three dimensions) is the one genuinely unwhiteboardable state and earns the 8-state build.

aha_moment.statement: Same polar bonds, but bending the molecule turns zero dipole into 1.85 debye.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: Water opens linear (arrows opposite, resultant zero, exactly like CO2) and bends to 104.5 degrees while the resultant arrow grows to 1.85 D.

STATE_1.title: One atom pulls the shared pair harder
STATE_1.label: Hydrogen chloride: the shared electron pair slides toward chlorine

tts_sentences.text_en: Hydrogen and chlorine share one electron pair.
Chlorine pulls harder: its electronegativity is 3.16, hydrogen's is 2.20, a difference of 0.96.
Watch the shared pair slide toward chlorine.
Chlorine becomes slightly negative, delta minus.
Hydrogen becomes slightly positive, delta plus.

STATE_2.title: The bond dipole arrow
STATE_2.label: HF's bond dipole drawn to scale, then swapped for HI

tts_sentences.text_en: A polar bond gets an arrow, drawn from delta plus to delta minus.
Its length is the measured dipole moment.
Hydrogen fluoride: electronegativity difference 1.78, dipole moment 1.83 debye, a long arrow.
Swap fluorine for iodine: the difference drops to 0.46, and the arrow shrinks to 0.45 debye.
A bigger difference gives a longer arrow.

STATE_3.title: Two arrows cancel — CO₂
STATE_3.label: Carbon dioxide: two long polar arrows sum to exactly zero

tts_sentences.text_en: Carbon dioxide is a straight molecule.
Each carbon-oxygen bond is strongly polar: both arrows are long.
Now add them as vectors.
They point in exactly opposite directions, so they cancel completely.
The total dipole moment is zero.
Polar bonds by themselves do not make a polar molecule.

misconception_watch.belief: If the bonds are polar, the molecule must be polar.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: Both carbon-oxygen arrows in CO2 are shown long and polar first — the wrong expectation's honest evidence — while the live HUD holds with no value shown yet; only afterward does a 'μ = 0 D' badge appear at the centre, together with the HUD reading 0.00 D, showing why.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Two polar bonds pointing in exactly opposite directions cancel completely, so the molecule ends up with no net dipole at all.

STATE_4.title: Bent water is polar
STATE_4.label: Water opens from a linear 180 degree pose and bends to 104.5, the resultant growing to 1.85 D

tts_sentences.text_en: Water has the same polar bonds, but the molecule is bent: its two lone pairs hold the bonds at 104.5 degrees.
The two arrows no longer point opposite ways.
Their sum is 1.85 debye — same bonds, different shape, polar molecule.
This is why a microwave oven heats food and leaves a dry plate cool.

STATE_5.title: Four arrows, still zero — CCl₄
STATE_5.label: Carbon tetrachloride: four polar C-Cl arrows sum to exactly zero, read under a full spin

tts_sentences.text_en: Four carbon-chlorine bonds, each polar, point at the four corners of a tetrahedron — the shape from the shapes lesson.
Turn the molecule: from every side the four arrows balance.
Their sum is exactly zero, in three dimensions.
Carbon tetrachloride has no dipole moment.
The symmetric shape makes the four arrows cancel.

misconception_watch.belief: Four polar bonds must add up to something — a board cannot show them cancelling, so surely they do not.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: Four polar C-Cl arrows are shown pointing at the four corners of a tetrahedron while the live HUD holds with no value shown yet; turning the molecule through a full rotation shows every side balances, and only then does the 'μ = 0 D' badge appear with the HUD reading 0.00 D.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: In three dimensions, four identical bonds pointing at the corners of a tetrahedron still cancel to zero, exactly like two opposite arrows do in a line.

STATE_6.title: One swap — CHCl₃
STATE_6.label: One chlorine of CCl4 replaced by hydrogen: the symmetry breaks and a resultant appears

tts_sentences.text_en: Carbon tetrachloride again: total zero.
Replace one chlorine with a hydrogen.
Three arrows keep their directions; the fourth is different.
The arrows no longer cancel — a resultant appears along the hydrogen-carbon axis.
This is chloroform, measured at 1.04 debye.
One substitution removes the symmetry.

STATE_7.title: Lone pair: NH₃ vs NF₃
STATE_7.label: Ammonia's bond arrows add to its lone pair; nitrogen trifluoride's oppose it

tts_sentences.text_en: Ammonia: nitrogen pulls harder than hydrogen, so the three bond arrows point toward nitrogen — the same way its lone pair points.
They add: 1.47 debye.
Swap the hydrogens for fluorines.
Fluorine pulls harder still, so the bond arrows now point away from nitrogen, against the lone pair.
Most of that cancels: 0.23 debye.

misconception_watch.belief: More polar bonds always mean a bigger molecular dipole moment.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The electronegativity difference (delta chi) rises from 0.84 to 0.94 and the bond arrows get longer, yet the resultant dipole moment falls from 1.47 D to 0.23 D — because the arrows now oppose the lone pair instead of adding to it.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: A more polar bond gives a longer arrow, but the molecule's dipole depends on the direction every arrow points, not just its length.

STATE_8.title: Explore polarity
STATE_8.label: Pick a molecule, change the angle or the halide, and watch the dipole moment respond

tts_sentences.text_en: Explore for yourself. Pick a molecule, change the bond angle or the halide, and watch the dipole moment respond.

regeneration_variants.label: Same vector-sum rule, boron trifluoride versus ammonia
regeneration_variants.physical_world: Boron trifluoride has three identical polar B-F bonds arranged in a flat triangle, exactly like carbon dioxide's two bonds are arranged in a straight line — the three bond dipoles cancel to zero. Ammonia has three polar N-H bonds arranged in a pyramid instead of a flat triangle, so its bond dipoles do not cancel.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Identical bond-dipole-vector-sum reasoning: a symmetric arrangement of identical polar bonds cancels to zero dipole moment; breaking that symmetry (a flat triangle becoming a pyramid) leaves a nonzero resultant.
